You use a reporting verb like to say or to tell about what someone said in a conversation.

For example: She said (that) my cat needed some additional tests.
When you tell people what someone has said in the past, you generally make the verb tense 'more in the past'. You need to change the verb to the next past form.

You have to change the pronoun if you are reporting what someone else said. Compare these two sentences. In each case the person actually said "I don't want to go."

• I said, “I don't want to go.” > I said I didn't want to go.
  • Bill said, “I don't want to go.” > Bill said he didn't want to go.
You usually introduce reported questions with the verb to ask.

The expert asked (me) if/whether ... (YES/NO questions)
The nurse asked (me) why/when/where/what/how ... (question-word questions)
You may need to change pronouns and tense as well as time and place in reported questions.
The word order is like that of a normal statement:

You often use the Simple Past and the Past Continuous tenses together.You use the Past Perfect tense to identify and talk about an ‘earlier past'.
I was just reading a legend about a Big Foot.
You can use the Simple Past tense to refer to a shorter action that happened in the middle of, or interrupted, the longer action.
We read a story about a legend around the camp fire.
When you are talking about a past event, you can refer to something that happened at an earlier time to that past event by using the Past Perfect tense.
The structure of the Past Perfect is:
I had believed that myths and legends were the same thing.

Which event happened first? I thought about setting up the alarm.
Which event happened later? I forgot.
You use the Past Perfect tense (not Simple Past) when you want to talk about how long something had continued up to a past moment.

images.text:
Everyone loves a good story. The art of storytelling has been a fixture in every culture since the beginning of civilization. Most people say that they had their own favorite story from their youth. Often, they found these stories frightening, exciting, and above all, engaging.

Myths and legends had offered listeners a glimpse into cultures, symbols and character and were used to help explain events in society. Experts have said, that myths and legends provided an insight into our fears and the state of society.

Many have asked about the differences between myths and legends.

We refer to ancient, traditional stories of heroes or gods as myths. In these tales, characters were forced to deal with problems or issues, explain a fact or handle a natural occurrence. People had used stories to explain universal and local beginnings and the existence of supernatural beings. Tales of Greek and Roman deities and heroes are commonly referred to as myths and have enthralled listeners throughout human history.

On the other hand, legends are stories that had passed down through generations. Legends are told as if they were historical events, rather than as an explanation for something or a symbolic narrative. Usually, they were created with some element of truth or fact, but they are surrounded with “mythical qualities.” Legends are often connected to a culture's spiritual beliefs. They involve heroic characters such as outlaw Robin Hood. He was stealing from the rich to give to the unfortunate.

Some have said that theses kind of stories had helped generations understand how people in the past saw, and understood, the world around them.
